      FAPD-AI: Slip Op. 24-53, dated May 1, 2024, is a Court of International Trade opinion and order by Judge Claire R. Kelly addressing consolidated motions for judgment on the agency record concerning the Department of Commerce's final determination in the 2019-2020 administrative review of the antidumping duty order on crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells from the People's Republic of China. The plaintiffs challenge 12 determinations, including Commerce's selection of Romanian HTS 7007.19.80 data to value solar glass, its valuation of ocean and air freight, its calculation of surrogate financial ratios, and its application of adverse facts available.       FAPD-AI: Slip Op. 25-67, dated May 30, 2025 and filed June 6, 2025, is a Court of International Trade opinion and order by Judge Claire R. Kelly reviewing Commerce's redetermination on remand in the eighth administrative review of the antidumping duty order on crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells from China. The court sustains Commerce's use of Freightos data to value air freight and remands Commerce's selection of Romanian HTS 7007.19.80 data to value solar glass and its calculation of an adverse inference using facts otherwise available. The opinion notes that plaintiffs challenged Commerce's decision to make no changes following the court's earlier remand order. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    Precision Planting LLC v. Maschio Gaspardo S.p.A. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-25-01809 / USCOURTS-ca13-25-01809-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit vacated the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decision in IPR2024-00008, which held that Precision Planting had not shown that claims 1-3, 7-12, and 16 of Maschio Gaspardo's U.S. Patent No. 8,770,121 would have been obvious, and remanded for further proceedings. The court held that the Board's finding that the Fiorido reference does not disclose a thrust-bearing element was not supported by substantial evidence. The court did not reach Precision Planting's challenges to the Board's motivation-to-combine analysis. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 20:52:28 Eastern time ET
    Faith Rashidiasl v. Upper Dublin School District (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01579 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01579-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit affirmed the Eastern District of Pennsylvania's dismissal of Faith Rashidiasl's amended complaint, which asserted Title VII, Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, and intentional infliction of emotional distress claims against the Upper Dublin School District and its counsel. The court held that the district court applied the correct plausibility standard under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii), did not abuse its discretion in denying further leave to amend, and would not consider arguments that were not developed in the briefing. The opinion is not precedential. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 20:52:28 Eastern time ET
    Ludwig Zelaya Romero v. Director Federal Bureau of Prisons, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01730 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01730-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit summarily affirmed the Western District of Pennsylvania's denial of Ludwig Criss Zelaya Romero's 28 U.S.C. § 2241 habeas petition, which sought First Step Act time credits. The court held that under 18 U.S.C. § 3632(d)(4)(E)(i), a federal prisoner who is the subject of a final order of removal is ineligible for those credits, and that the expedited removal order issued against him in November 2024 became final on issuance because it was not subject to administrative appeal. The opinion is not precedential. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 20:52:28 Eastern time ET
    Green Trevor v. Mumin, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01851 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01851-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit affirmed the Eastern District of Pennsylvania's dismissal with prejudice of Green Muniyr Trevor's amended complaint, which raised constitutional and other claims against Pennsylvania and school district officials and a charter school arising from a school dress code policy. The court held that the complaint did not plausibly allege a First Amendment free exercise violation, a substantive due process violation, or a Contract Clause violation, and it did not consider arguments raised for the first time on appeal or claims the appellant abandoned. The opinion is not precedential. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit reversed the District of Delaware's award of $9.1 million in attorneys' fees to Elysium Health, Inc. under 35 U.S.C. § 285, concluding that the district court abused its discretion.   • Observed at 20:52:22 Eastern time ET
    Cozy Inn, Incorporated, et al v. City of Salina, Kansas (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-03225 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-03225-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the District of Kansas's grant of summary judgment to Cozy Inn and Stephen Howard on First Amendment claims against the City of Salina, Kansas, concerning the city's sign code and its handling of a sign permit application for a painted wall display. The opinion explains that the sign code requires permits for signs, while murals are not regulated, and that the city placed the permit application on hold in February 2024. The plaintiffs had sought a declaration that the sign code and its enforcement are a content-based restriction on speech and an unlawful prior restraint. The court exercised jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and affirmed. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-26-7231 / USCOURTS-ca9-26-7231-0

    FAPD-AI: The Ninth Circuit denied the United States' emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal in United States v. California, which sought an order requiring California and Los Angeles County to sequester and verify the citizenship of vote-by-mail ballots from individuals identified as likely noncitizens. The panel held that it has appellate jurisdiction over the denial of the temporary restraining order and concluded that the United States had not shown that the law and facts clearly favor its position under 18 U.S.C. § 611 and the Elections Clause. The order notes a dissent by Judge Bumatay, and the remainder of the merits analysis is truncated in the source text. USCOURTS-SEL-01
